title: In the interview
summary: How to describe a full sprint in Azure DevOps, translate to and from Jira terms, and answer the common questions without overclaiming.

lessons.title: Describing a sprint end to end
lessons.body:
The most common Azure DevOps interview prompt is some version of 'walk me through how your team ran a sprint'. A strong answer is a story in order, with the tool woven in and one or two real decisions. Aim for about two minutes.

**A structure that works:**

1. **Before the sprint (refinement).** 'I owned the product backlog in Boards. I wrote stories with acceptance criteria and ordered them by priority, and groomed the top ones with developers so they were estimated.'
2. **Planning.** 'On the first day we set capacity for each person, pulled stories into the sprint, and developers broke them into tasks with hour estimates. We agreed a sprint goal.'
3. **During the sprint.** 'Daily standup at the taskboard. Developers linked branches and pull requests to stories. When a build was ready on the test environment, I ran the test cases in Test Plans linked to each story, and logged bugs from failed steps, linked back to the story.'
4. **Visibility.** 'A shared dashboard with burndown, open bugs and test progress, so stakeholders could see status without asking.'
5. **End of sprint.** 'Review of finished stories with the customer's staff, UAT for larger releases, then a retrospective. Unfinished work went back to the backlog and I re-prioritized.'
6. **A concrete decision.** 'In one sprint the SOS alert story grew once we found notifications needed a radius filter. We saw it in the burndown mid-sprint, deferred a lower-priority story and told the customer.'

**Make it yours.** Replace anything above that did not happen exactly that way. The strongest answers use specific details you really remember: the name of a feature, how many people, a number such as ticket inflow dropping 35% after the documentation rewrite.

**Watch for:**

- Saying 'we' for everything. Say 'I' for what you did and 'the team' for what they did.
- Listing features of the tool instead of telling what happened.
- Overclaiming: you facilitated planning, standups and retrospectives; you did not hold a Scrum Master role or certification.

Practice it aloud. If the full version runs longer than two and a half minutes, cut the tool detail and keep the decisions.
keyPoints: Tell the sprint in order: refine, plan, run, make visible, review and retro.
Include one specific decision or problem you handled.
Use 'I' for your actions and 'the team' for theirs.
Do not claim Scrum Master title or certification.
Keep it to about two minutes.
lessons.interviewAngle: This is the core answer for most coordinator, BA, PO and QA roles. Make the tool the setting, not the subject. Mention Boards, Test Plans, Repos links and the dashboard naturally, and give one real number or incident so it sounds lived rather than recited.

exercises.prompt: Which is the strongest way to answer 'walk me through a sprint'?
choices: List every Azure DevOps feature you know
Tell it in order from refinement to retrospective, including one real decision
Say the process is the same everywhere
exercises.explanation: A sequential story with a concrete decision shows lived experience, which a feature list does not.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is honest and safe given your experience?
choices: I was the Scrum Master for the team
I facilitated sprint planning, standups and retrospectives as project manager and backlog owner
I administered the Azure DevOps organization
exercises.explanation: You ran these ceremonies but did not hold the Scrum Master title or admin the tools.

exercises.prompt: Before sprint planning, what is the name of the activity of clarifying and estimating the top backlog items?
exercises.explanation: Refinement makes top items clear, estimated and small enough for the sprint.

exercises.prompt: Write a spoken answer, about 150 to 220 words, to 'Walk me through how a sprint ran on your team in Azure DevOps.' Use your real experience with the pharmacist scheduling product, include one decision, and keep the claims honest.
exercises.answer:
"We ran two-week sprints in Azure DevOps. Before each sprint I groomed the backlog in Boards: I wrote the user stories and acceptance criteria and ordered them, then reviewed the top items with the developers so they were estimated. In sprint planning we set capacity for each person, pulled in stories, and the developers split them into tasks with hour estimates. We agreed a sprint goal.

During the sprint we did a short daily standup at the taskboard. Developers linked their branches and pull requests to the stories. When a build reached the test environment, I ran the linked test cases in Test Plans and logged bugs from failed steps, linked to the story. A dashboard with burndown, open bugs and test progress meant our customer didn't have to ask for status.

One sprint, the SOS alert story grew once we realized we needed a radius filter. We saw it in the burndown by midweek, deferred a lower-priority story and told the customer why. At the end we reviewed finished work and held a retrospective, and anything unfinished went back to the backlog."
rubric: Covers refinement, planning, execution, visibility and review/retro in order
Names Boards and Test Plans accurately
Includes one concrete decision or problem
Uses honest I/we language without Scrum Master or admin claims
Stays within a reasonable spoken length

lessons.title: Mapping to Jira and common questions
lessons.body:
Many employers use Jira, and you have used both tools at the same level. The ideas map closely, so interviewers mainly want to know whether you can move between them.

| Azure DevOps | Jira |
|---|---|
| Organization / Project | Site / Project |
| Work item | Issue |
| User Story / PBI / Issue (by template) | Story |
| Epic, Feature | Epic (Jira has Epic; Feature is often a label or a custom level) |
| Task, Bug | Task/Sub-task, Bug |
| Iteration path / Sprint | Sprint |
| Area path | Component (roughly) |
| Backlog | Backlog |
| Kanban board / Taskboard | Board (Kanban or Scrum) |
| Work item query | JQL filter |
| Dashboard and widgets | Dashboard and gadgets |
| Repos, Pipelines | Usually a separate tool, such as Bitbucket or GitHub, with Jira integration |
| Test Plans | Not built in; Jira uses add-ons for test management |
| Linked work items | Linked issues |

The differences to mention: in Azure DevOps source control, builds and testing are part of the same product, while Jira is mainly planning and relies on connected tools. Jira workflows and issue types are configured per project; Azure DevOps ties these to the process template.

**Common questions and how to approach them:**

- *'Which have you used more?'* Equal daily use; keep it factual.
- *'What do you like about Azure DevOps?'* Traceability from story to test to code in one place.
- *'What frustrated you?'* Something real and minor, such as the number of fields on a bug form or navigating between services, framed with how you worked around it.
- *'How do you handle bugs in the backlog?'* Link to the story, triage in grooming, and prioritize alongside new work.
- *'Can you set up a project?'* 'I haven't administered either tool, but I know what configuration decisions are involved and I'm comfortable learning.'

**Learning a new tool quickly.** Say what you do: find the equivalent of backlog, board, query and test management, then copy the team's existing conventions before suggesting changes.
keyPoints: Work item = issue; iteration = sprint; query = JQL filter; area path roughly = component.
Azure DevOps bundles repos, pipelines and test plans; Jira connects to separate tools.
Equal daily use of both tools; no admin claims for either.
For 'what frustrated you?' pick something real and minor, with your workaround.
lessons.interviewAngle: If the employer uses Jira, say your Azure DevOps habits transfer and map the key terms out loud. If they use Azure DevOps, lean into traceability and Test Plans. In both cases be upfront that you are a daily user, not an administrator, and give a short plan for learning their configuration in the first week.

exercises.prompt: Which Azure DevOps concept is closest to a Jira sprint?
exercises.explanation: A sprint is an iteration in Azure DevOps. Area path is closer to a component.

exercises.prompt: What is the Jira equivalent of an Azure DevOps work item query?
exercises.explanation: JQL (Jira Query Language) filters play the role of saved queries.

exercises.prompt: An interviewer asks whether you can set up an Azure DevOps project and permissions. What is the honest answer?
choices: I haven't administered it; I'm a daily user and can learn the configuration side
That's not something PMs ever do
exercises.explanation: Be accurate about your level and show willingness to learn.

exercises.prompt: The hiring team uses Jira with a separate test management add-on. Write a 100 to 150 word answer to 'You've used Azure DevOps. How quickly could you be productive in Jira?' that maps at least five terms and states honestly what you would need to learn.
exercises.answer: "Quickly, I think, because the ideas are the same and I have used both daily at a similar level. What I called a work item is an issue in Jira, a user story is a story, an iteration path is a sprint, and my saved queries would become JQL filters. Boards and backlogs work the same way, and linked work items are linked issues. The difference I would watch for is that Jira usually relies on connected tools for source control and testing, where Azure DevOps has them built in, so I would learn how your team connects code and test management. I would also need a week or two to learn your workflows and JQL syntax. I have not administered either tool, so I would follow your existing conventions first."
rubric: Maps at least five terms correctly
Notes the built-in versus connected tools difference
States what needs to be learned (workflows, JQL, integrations)
